question: On a certain math exam, \(10\%\) of the students got \(70\) points, \(25\%\) got \(80\) points, \(20\%\) got \(85\) points, \(15\%\) got \(90\) points, and the rest got \(95\) points. What is the difference between the mean and the median score on this exam?
solution:
The percentage scoring \(95\) is
\[
100\%-10\%-25\%-20\%-15\%=30\%.
\]
To find the mean, weight each score by the fraction of students who earned it:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{mean}
&=0.10(70)+0.25(80)+0.20(85)\\
&\quad+0.15(90)+0.30(95)\\
&=7+20+17+13.5+28.5\\
&=86.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the median, imagine the scores sorted from least to greatest. The first \(10\%+25\%=35\%\) are below \(85\), and the next \(20\%\) equal \(85\). Thus the middle positions lie in the group scoring \(85\), so the median is \(85\).

The difference is \(86-85=\boxed{1}\) point, choice \(\mathrm{B}\).

edges.reason: Percentage weights are common and percent meaning helps interpret them. Integer frequencies and raw ratio weights supply equally valid weighted means without percentages.
Explaining weights changes how observations contribute to an average level; the ordinary mean supplies that averaging meaning, restricted to this interpretation component.
edges.scope: weighted mean as generalization of arithmetic mean

edges.reason: The median criterion orders the supplied numerical data and is not restricted to nonnegative scores. Claude's claim about most datasets does not justify excluding legitimate negative values. Retain rational-order content for that scope, without making every number-line/absolute-value comparison technique compulsory.
edges.scope: Ordering rational-valued data, including negative values, to identify the median

edges.reason: The source explicitly defines an even-sized median as the arithmetic mean of the middle two values; no mean is needed for the odd-sized case or mode alone.
